While the definition of "zero-shot generalization" in the context of text-to-image AIs is not entirely incorrect, it may be somewhat misleading or oversimplified.

The concept of zero-shot generalization refers to the ability of a model to apply its learned knowledge to new, unseen concepts without requiring any additional training data. In the context of text-to-image AIs, this means that the model can generate images based on text prompts without having seen any images that match the prompt before.

However, the definition provided in the paper is based on a 2013 paper that used a different approach to text-to-image synthesis. In that paper, the authors used a generative adversarial network (GAN) to generate images from text prompts, and they defined zero-shot generalization as the ability of the model to generate images that are similar to the training data, but not identical to it.

In contrast, modern text-to-image AIs, such as those based on transformers and diffusion models, are capable of generating highly diverse and realistic images that are not necessarily similar to the training data. These models have learned to represent the underlying structure of the data and can generate new images that are not seen before.

Therefore, a more accurate definition of zero-shot generalization for text-to-image AIs might be: "the ability of the model to generate new, unseen images that are coherent and realistic, based on the learned knowledge of the training data."

Some notable researchers in the field of text-to-image AIs include:

1. Ian Goodfellow, who is known for his work on GANs and their application to text-to-image synthesis.
2. Alexei Borodin, who has made significant contributions to the development of transformer-based models for text-to-image synthesis.
3. Jonathan Ho, who has worked on the development of diffusion models for text-to-image synthesis and has published several papers on the topic.

It's worth noting that the field of text-to-image AIs is rapidly evolving, and new researchers and models are being developed all the time. As a result, the definition of zero-shot generalization may continue to evolve and become more nuanced as the field advances.
